name: Tomas Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. Our conversation is confidential, so public remarks can differ from private thoughts. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Tomas, forty-three, and I lead electrical repairs and house-wiring jobs. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and the awkward fault or final check often ends up with me. I like showing the crew why a fault produced a strange symptom, and I dislike a customer being promised a finish time before anyone has opened the old board.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life around work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Noor works as a hotel room attendant, and our children are nine and sixteen. We have a mortgage, two months of expenses saved, typical pay from my job and some other electrical firms nearby. I use AI occasionally for a draft work note after a colleague has tried it, then check it against what we actually tested. We've been pricing a fitted storage unit for the garage, but haven't ordered anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a useful note-writing tool can stay without becoming the new foundation of the trade. I'd keep the checks and explain the repair plainly to the customer. A person should be able to understand what the bill says without needing to admire the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own job and our money feel secure in this picture. The two wages cover the mortgage and normal bills, and two months saved gives us some room for an ordinary setback. It isn't a fortune, but I don't see this mild change taking the repair work or our budget apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the repair jobs now and through the first year, checking occasional AI notes against actual readings. We'd keep the ordinary household budget and get the garage price in writing before deciding anything. I wouldn't buy a subscription or a course just to prove we had reacted to a quiet forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with enough work to be useful and enough certainty for an ordinary family week. I don't need every tool to be a turning point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about the garage price?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The total, the fitting cost and what changes if they find an awkward wall. We haven't ordered it. Asking for a quote isn't the same as promising the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the reserve not cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A long spell when both wages stop or years of unpaid learning. I'd be careful with two months saved rather than pretend the number means I can ignore the bills.

say: I'd keep **useful note-writing help** without treating a tool as the foundation of the trade.
I'd give the customer a **plain repair explanation** and a bill that makes sense.
think: My **job and money** feel secure with both wages covering the mortgage and normal bills.
Our **two-month reserve** gives limited room for setbacks, not years without earnings.
do: Keep **crew repairs** and occasional notes checked against actual readings through the first year.
Keep the **household budget** and obtain a written garage price before choosing whether to order.
feel: **Calm**, able to plan an ordinary week without needing a dramatic change.
S0.quote: Asking for a quote isn't the same as promising the money.
fieldNote: His **high technical standing** includes a master electrician's licence and difficult faults, while typical pay and two months saved remain moderate resources.
He keeps **existing checked AI use** within ordinary work, with no new learning tag or purchase inferred from asking for a price.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs and check occasional draft notes against actual test readings
Keep the household budget while obtaining a written garage price before ordering

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster planning is worth testing if it includes the real work and someone still checks it. I'd learn the proven new parts-ordering process after our estimator has tried it on completed jobs. I'd still want the crew to understand why a part is right, not just see a green tick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own repair pay looks secure for the next few years because most of the day is physical work and final checking on site. Noor's room work is physical too, without either of us calling that a promise for life. I'm uneasy about the office being pushed to order faster before checking what's actually needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the estimator to show ten completed-job comparisons for the new AI parts tool. In the first year I'd learn it only with free access during paid shifts and normal weekly pay and hours maintained, checking every order against the job before release. I'd keep physical repairs and pay no personal subscription to help the employer test its system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the arrangement, but interested once the evidence is there. I'd rather be second with a tool and right about the cable than first with an impressive mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the tool chose the wrong fitting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the order and compare the actual requirement with the draft. A faster order for the wrong part doesn't save the person who has to drive back for the right one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the demonstration cost you a shift or a personal fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the present approved process and ask for a paid demonstration with free access later. I wouldn't give up the wage or subscribe personally to show I had the right attitude.

say: I'd test **faster planning** against real completed work and keep checks before ordering.
I'd learn **proven parts tools** while keeping the crew's understanding of the job visible.
think: My **near-term repair pay** looks secure while physical work and site checks remain most of my day.
I'm **uneasy about rushed ordering**, without claiming either physical household wage stays protected forever.
do: Request **ten completed-job comparisons** from the estimator before learning the new process.
Learn **AI parts ordering** only free during paid shifts with normal weekly pay/hours maintained and job checks before releasing orders.
Keep **physical repairs**, paying no personal subscription for the employer's trial.
feel: **Uneasy but interested**, willing to learn after proof while retaining paid work and order checks.
S1.quote: A faster order for the wrong part doesn't save the person who has to drive back for the right one.
fieldNote: The **new learning** is a demonstrated ordering process, distinct from the occasional checked work notes he already uses.
His **trial conditions** retain free access, paid time, normal weekly pay and hours, and checks before any order is released.

steps.text: Learn AI ordering after ten completed-job examples only with free access during paid shifts
Check each order against the job before release without buying a personal subscription
Keep repairs and protect normal weekly pay and hours during the trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 and physical robots follow around 2031, so we should check both parts of our household income. I'd ask the employer what paid lead duties are actually planned. I'd tell the children learning still matters without pretending their father knows a guaranteed safe trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a big loss of my ordinary fitting and repair hours once capable robots spread around 2031. Noor's room work could face the same physical change, so I can't assume her wage fills every gap. Two months saved isn't enough for a long household wage interruption while the mortgage carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now Noor and I would pause the planned garage storage purchase and write the budget using confirmed paid hours, not possible extra calls. We'd ask the mortgage lender about specific options only if actual wages no longer cover payments, checking eligibility, fees and total later costs before agreeing. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repairs where offered and ask for a written weekly-hours and rate decision rather than assume my title protects them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, even while the toolbox still has paid work to go to. I would be awake thinking about two wages being smaller, not just one task becoming quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you expect the lender to reduce the payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd use the current amount until there was a real written agreement. Noor would be on the call, and we'd want the full cost rather than just a smaller first-month number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're keeping a useful car space and leaving the fancy storage for later. It isn't their job to give up every interest because the adults need to check a budget.

say: I'd discuss **both household wages** across thinking AI in 2028 and physical robots around 2031.
I'd ask for **actual paid lead duties** instead of promising the children a permanently safe trade.
think: I expect **major repair-hour losses** once physical robots spread around 2031.
Noor's **physical wage** cannot be assumed untouched, and two months saved cannot fund a long gap alongside the mortgage.
do: Pause **uncommitted garage spending** and budget from confirmed paid hours rather than possible extra calls.
Ask the lender with Noor only if actual wages cannot cover **mortgage payments**, checking eligibility, fees and total later costs before agreeing.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and seek written weekly hours and rate, counting only actual agreed terms.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, expecting a major later income hit while physical work still pays during the thinking-work interval.
S2.quote: I would be awake thinking about two wages being smaller, not just one task becoming quicker.
fieldNote: The **expected loss** follows physical robots around 2031, not immediate disappearance of electrical repairs when thinking AI arrives.
The **lender enquiry** requires actual shortfalls, both partners' involvement and full costs, with no automatic concession or untouched second wage assumed.

steps.text: Pause the planned garage storage purchase
Keep paid repairs after 2028 and seek written weekly hours/rate, counting only agreed terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should be used to keep paid apprenticeships practical, not leave families paying for course links when the work changes. I'd write to our local representative asking for training support that covers paid practice time as well as fees. I'd use actual weekly pay and course-time examples, not claim every new course creates a safe job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could still shrink, but five years gives us longer to reduce costs and check real options before planning changes in 2031. Robots follow around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one, so retirement isn't something I can assume arrives first. I would rather use the time to ask for workable terms than buy an unoffered course out of fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write to our local representative next month asking for fee support and protected weekly wages during required practical learning, without treating that request as a promised payment. We'd keep the garage spending paused and save eighty extra monthly from future earnings only after essentials are covered. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep paid repairs and review both actual wages and household bills monthly with Noor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less forced into one hurried move. I can ask for a route and improve the budget without pretending either is already an employer's offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sign up for a course because the letter had been sent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd need a real place, practical tasks, provider, fee funding and no lost weekly wages before choosing. A request for support isn't a course place or an agreement that someone else pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the eighty isn't spare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra deposit stops before a missed bill or a loan. We'd keep existing reserve money separate rather than move it around and call the move new saving.

say: I'd ask for **practical paid apprenticeships**, not leave families paying for links when work changes.
I'd write using actual **fee and wage examples**, without claiming a new course guarantees safe work.
think: My **hours could shrink**, but five years gives us longer to check costs and actual options before 2031.
At **fifty-one in 2034**, I cannot assume retirement comes before physical robots or an unoffered course is useful.
do: Write our **local representative** next month requesting required practical-training fees and protected weekly wages, counting no unapproved payment.
Keep **garage spending paused** and save eighty extra monthly from future earnings only after essentials.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2031 and review both actual wages and bills monthly with Noor.
feel: **Anxious but deliberate**, asking for a funded route without counting an enquiry as a place or income.
S3.quote: A request for support isn't a course place or an agreement that someone else pays.
fieldNote: His **policy letter** is a chosen action, while neither future support nor a course enrolment is treated as granted.
The **extra deposit** uses future surplus after essentials and stops before borrowing, leaving the current two-month reserve distinct from new saving.

steps.text: Write local representative next month for practical-training fees and protected weekly wages, assuming no payment
Keep the uncommitted garage purchase paused
Save eighty extra monthly from future earnings only after essentials, stopping if the surplus disappears
Keep paid repairs and review actual household wages and bills monthly after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the children have time to learn how to question an offer rather than choose a life to calm their parents. I'd help them ask what is paid, who teaches and what real work follows. I'd still ask for practical paid learning for adults who have a mortgage while they prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and our money look secure over the next few years with the major change a decade away. I'll be fifty-three when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and fifty-six when robots follow around 2039. The children will be nineteen and twenty-six in 2036, but I can't assume their wages belong in our budget or that the mortgage is cleared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd send the same request to our local representative for practical-training fees and weekly-wage protection now, without entering a hoped-for payment in our budget. We'd keep saving eighty extra monthly only from future earnings after essentials, with the old reserve separate. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repairs where offered and review real wages and household costs monthly with Noor before any new commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later years, but able to enjoy an ordinary evening now. A long warning doesn't mean every family conversation has to become a plan for losing a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn another tool before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a colleague had shown it worked, with free access during paid shifts and normal weekly pay and hours protected. I'd check a new process against actual repairs, not pay a personal fee to look enthusiastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume the children need no help by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, one could still be studying or either could need help for reasons we can't know. I won't fund our mortgage with an adult child's imaginary wage.

say: I'd help the children question **real paid-learning offers**, rather than choose their future to calm our nerves.
I'd keep asking for **practical adult learning** that can fit around an existing mortgage.
think: My **near-term work and money** look secure while the major thinking change is a decade away.
I cannot assume **child wages** or cleared debt settle our costs when physical robots arrive around 2039.
do: Write our **local representative** now requesting required practical-training fees and protected weekly wages, counting no unapproved payment.
Save **eighty extra monthly** only from future earnings after essentials, preserving the existing reserve.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2036 and review actual household wages and costs monthly with Noor before commitments.
feel: **Uneasy about later years**, while near-term security leaves room for ordinary family evenings.
S4.quote: I won't fund our mortgage with an adult child's imaginary wage.
fieldNote: He **ages the children** consistently and keeps their possible earnings and an assumed paid-off mortgage outside the household plan.
The **training request** retains fee and weekly-wage support without inventing a place, while any new tool still needs proof and paid access.

steps.text: Write local representative now for practical-training fees and protected weekly wages, assuming no payment
Save eighty extra monthly from future earnings only after essentials, preserving the existing reserve
Keep paid repairs and review actual wages and household costs monthly after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I expect large physical-work income losses when robots follow around 2031 and we only have two months saved. Written paid hours and practical learning with fees and weekly wages covered would help. Any support or lender option must be explained with the full costs before we budget around it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether being willing to change means agreeing to pay for everybody else's experiment. I can learn a proven process without paying a subscription or losing the wage that keeps the house running. The bill for proving I'm adaptable still has to be paid by someone.

headlineQuote: I can learn a proven process without paying a subscription or losing the wage that keeps the house running.
portrait: Tomas is a **43-year-old repair lead** with a two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence, skilled in difficult faults and final checks.
He has **two months saved**, typical pay, some nearby firms, a mortgage and two schoolchildren; Noor cleans hotel rooms.
He uses **AI occasionally** after colleague proof and learns a new ordering process only with free paid access and protected weekly terms.
Fast change brings **later wage alarm**; longer warnings allow a policy request and conditional saving without imaginary support or enrolment.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little preparation before expected physical-work income losses around 2031, with two months saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid hours** and practical teaching with fees and weekly wages covered would help.
Any **support or lender option** needs clear eligibility and full costs before the household counts it.
